lessons.title: The Nature of God & the Trinity

before.content_html:
The Nature of God

Christians are monotheistic — they believe in one God who created and sustains everything. Although God is called “Father,” Christians do not believe God has a physical body or a gender. God is a spirit, beyond human understanding, and is considered holy — completely pure, set apart and worthy of worship.

The Nicene Creed, recited by Christians worldwide, opens with the words: “We believe in One God.” Christians believe this one God has several key qualities that together make God perfect. Three of these qualities are central to the AQA specification: God as omnipotent, God as loving (benevolent), and God as just.

God as Omnipotent

Omnipotent means all-powerful. Christians believe God has unlimited power and authority — nothing is beyond what God can do. God demonstrated this power by creating the entire universe from nothing and continues to sustain all life.

Key Fact

“Nothing is impossible with God.” (Luke 1:37) — These words were spoken by the Angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary. Christians use this verse to show that God’s power has absolutely no limits.

Belief in God’s omnipotence influences Christians in several ways. When they see the complexity of nature, they see evidence of a powerful creator. It also means they trust that God can perform miracles, and it gives them confidence when they pray that God has the power to answer.

God as Loving (Benevolent)

Benevolent means all-loving and all-good. Christians believe God loves every human being unconditionally. God created humans out of love and wants to share that love with all creation.

Key Fact

“God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16) — Christians see sending Jesus as the greatest act of God’s love.

This belief helps Christians feel valued and gives them a purpose — to share God’s love with others through kindness, charity and forgiveness. Because God is all-loving, Christians believe God forgives those who are truly sorry for their sins.

God as Just

Christians believe God is a just (fair) judge of all humanity. Because God is all-powerful and all-loving, God is the perfect giver of justice. This means God will never support injustice, oppression, prejudice or cruelty.

“God is just: He will pay back trouble to those who trouble you.” (2 Thessalonians 1:6) — This teaches Christians that God sees all actions and will judge everyone fairly. No wrongdoing will go unnoticed. Because of this, Christians are motivated to fight against injustice wherever they encounter it.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

If God is omnipotent, loving and just, why does evil and suffering exist? This is called the problem of evil, and it is one of the biggest challenges to Christian belief.

The problem can be stated simply: if God is loving, he would want to stop suffering; if God is powerful, he could stop suffering; if God is just, he would not allow injustice. Yet suffering clearly exists. The philosopher David Hume called this the “inconsistent triad” — the three ideas seem to contradict each other.

Christians distinguish between two types of evil. Moral evil is caused by human actions — murder, theft, war and cruelty. Natural evil is caused by the natural world — earthquakes, disease, floods and famine.

Free will: God gave humans the freedom to choose how to live. Some choose to do wrong, causing moral evil. Christians argue that genuine free will is better than being puppets, even if some misuse it.

Life as a test: Some Christians believe suffering tests faith. The story of Job shows that God allows suffering to test whether people remain faithful — and rewards those who do.

Part of God’s plan: Humans cannot fully understand God’s reasons. “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5) suggests God has a purpose for every person, even if suffering seems unfair.

The Devil: Some Christians believe Satan tempts people into sin. Evil is caused by the Devil, not by God — though this raises the question of why God allows the Devil to operate.

The Oneness of God and the Trinity

Although Christians believe in one God, they understand God as existing in three persons: Father, Son (Jesus Christ) and Holy Spirit. This is called the Trinity. It does not mean there are three separate gods — the three persons are all fully God, sharing one divine nature.

Key Fact

The Trinity is one God in three persons: the Father (creator and sustainer), the Son (Jesus Christ, who became human to save humanity), and the Holy Spirit (God’s presence active in the world today). All three are equal and eternal.

God the Father is the creator and sustainer of all life. He is the source of all things and the one to whom Christians direct their prayers. Jesus taught his followers to pray “Our Father.”

God the Son is Jesus Christ. Christians believe the Son has always existed with the Father but took human form (the incarnation) to live among people, teach them about God, and die on the cross to save humanity from sin.

God the Holy Spirit is the unseen power of God at work in the world. Christians believe the Holy Spirit guides, comforts and strengthens believers. At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended on the disciples as tongues of fire (Acts 2), empowering them to spread the Christian message.

The Nicene Creed affirms the Trinity: “We believe in one God, the Father Almighty… And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God… And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Giver of Life.” The Trinity is central to Christian worship — Christians are baptised “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Some Christians find the Trinity difficult to understand. Common analogies include water existing as ice, liquid and steam (three forms, one substance), or the sun giving light, heat and energy. However, these analogies are imperfect — the Trinity is considered a mystery that humans can only partly grasp.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes God as omnipotent?
A) God is all-loving
B) God is all-powerful
C) God is all-knowing
D) God is everywhere
practice_questions.marks: The correct answer is B. Omnipotent means all-powerful — God has unlimited authority and power. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the three persons of the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. [1 mark for all three named correctly]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in God as loving (benevolent) influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Christians feel valued and loved by God, which gives them confidence and self-worth. They believe God cares about them individually, which brings comfort in difficult times.
• Christians are motivated to share God’s love with others through practical acts of kindness, charity work and forgiveness — imitating the unconditional love God shows them.
• Because God is all-loving, Christians believe in forgiveness. This influences them to forgive others who wrong them, just as God forgives those who repent.
• John 3:16 teaches that God loved the world enough to send Jesus. This influences Christians to make sacrifices for others.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about the nature of God. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• God is omnipotent — all-powerful. Supported by Luke 1:37: ‘Nothing is impossible with God.’ This was spoken by the Angel Gabriel to Mary, showing God’s power has no limits. (1–2 marks)
• God is benevolent — all-loving. Supported by John 3:16: ‘God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son.’ Sending Jesus is seen as God’s greatest act of love. (1–2 marks)
• God is just — fair. Supported by 2 Thessalonians 1:6: ‘God is just: He will pay back trouble to those who trouble you.’ (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied to the belief for additional marks.
Two beliefs, each explained and supported by a source of authority. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The problem of evil and suffering proves that God does not exist.’
Evaluate this statement considering arguments for and against. In your response you should:
• refer to Christian teachings
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the statement:
• If God is all-powerful and all-loving, he would want to and be able to stop suffering — yet suffering exists.
• David Hume’s inconsistent triad: God cannot be omnipotent, benevolent and allow evil to exist simultaneously.
• Natural evil (earthquakes, disease) cannot be blamed on human free will, making it harder to explain.
Arguments against the statement:
• Moral evil is explained by free will — God gave humans genuine choice, and some misuse it. This is not God’s fault.
• Suffering may be a test of faith. The story of Job shows God rewards those who remain faithful through suffering.
• God’s plan is beyond human understanding — ‘Before I formed you in the womb I knew you’ (Jeremiah 1:5).
• Belief in God brings hope and comfort through suffering, especially the promise of eternal life.
Top band (10-12): Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view. Logical chains of reasoning supported by knowledge. References to religion applied to the issue.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasoned consideration of different points of view with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Reasoned consideration of a point of view. OR Recognition of different points of view. Max Level 2 if no reference to religion.
Lower band (1-3): Point of view with reason(s) stated.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the belief in the Trinity influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Christians are baptised ‘in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit’ (Matthew 28:19). This shows the Trinity is central to how Christians enter the faith and shapes their worship practices.
• Belief in the Holy Spirit gives Christians confidence that God is active in the world today — guiding, comforting and strengthening them in daily life and decision-making.
• The Trinity helps Christians understand God’s relationship with humanity: the Father as creator, the Son as saviour, and the Spirit as ongoing guide.
• Christians recite the Nicene Creed which affirms the Trinity, uniting believers across different denominations in a shared statement of faith.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

before.content_html:
Christian Beliefs About Creation

Christians believe God created the entire universe. The two main biblical accounts of creation are found in Genesis 1 and John 1:1–3. Both are important For the exam , and students must understand different Christian interpretations of these texts.

Genesis 1:1–3 — The Creation Account

The book of Genesis describes God creating the world in six days and resting on the seventh. “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Now the earth was formless and empty, darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters. And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:1–3)

Key Fact

Genesis 1 shows the role of both the Word and the Spirit in creation. God’s Spirit hovered over the waters (the Holy Spirit was present), and God spoke creation into existence (“God said”) — this is the Word (Logos) at work. Christians see this as evidence that the Trinity was active at creation.

John 1:1–3 — The Word (Logos)

The Gospel of John opens with a different perspective on creation: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. Through him all things were made; without him nothing was made that has been made.” (John 1:1–3)

Christians understand “the Word” as referring to Jesus Christ (God the Son). This passage teaches that Jesus was not just a human teacher — he existed with God from the very beginning and played an active role in creating everything. Nothing that exists was made without him.

Taken together, Genesis 1 and John 1 show that all three persons of the Trinity were involved in creation. God the Father initiated creation. God the Son (the Word) was the agent through whom everything was made. God the Holy Spirit was present, hovering over the waters. This is significant because it shows the Trinity working together from the very beginning of time.

Different Interpretations of Creation

Christians disagree about how to interpret the creation accounts. The AQA exam expects you to understand these different views:

Literalist (fundamentalist) view: Some Christians believe the Genesis account is literally true — God created the world in six 24-hour days exactly as described. They reject the theory of evolution and believe the Earth is only a few thousand years old. They see the Bible as the direct word of God, without error.

Liberal (non-literal) view: Many Christians interpret the creation story as a myth or metaphor — it communicates important truths (that God is the creator, that creation is good, that humans are special) without being a scientific account. They accept the theory of evolution and the Big Bang as the mechanism God used. The “six days” may represent long periods of time.

Catholic view: The Catholic Church teaches that faith and science are not in conflict. Pope Francis has said that the Big Bang and evolution are real, but God is behind them. The creation stories reveal why God created (out of love), not how the physical process worked.

Key Fact

All Christians agree that God is the ultimate creator of everything. They disagree about how to interpret the Genesis account — literally (six 24-hour days) or non-literally (metaphorical, compatible with science). The exam often tests these “common and divergent views.”

Christian Beliefs About the Afterlife

Christians believe that physical death is not the end. What happens after death is a central part of Christian faith, and different Christians hold different views about the details.

Resurrection and Life After Death

Resurrection is the belief that the dead will be raised to new life. Christians believe this because Jesus himself was resurrected three days after his crucifixion. St Paul wrote: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17) — showing that resurrection is absolutely central to Christianity.

Some Christians believe in bodily resurrection — that the physical body will be raised and transformed. Others believe in spiritual resurrection — that the soul lives on in a new spiritual form. Catholics believe the body and soul are reunited at the resurrection on the last day.

Judgement

Christians believe God will judge every person after death. Some Christians distinguish between two types of judgement:

Particular judgement: This happens immediately after a person dies. Their soul is judged by God and sent to heaven, hell or (in Catholic belief) purgatory.

Final (Last) judgement: At the end of time, Jesus will return and judge all people — both the living and the dead. This is described in Matthew 25:31–46, the parable of the sheep and the goats, where those who helped others are welcomed into God’s kingdom and those who did not are sent away.

Heaven and Hell

Heaven is understood as a state of eternal happiness and peace in the presence of God. It is the ultimate reward for those who have lived according to God’s will. Jesus told the criminal crucified beside him: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Hell is understood as eternal separation from God. Some Christians believe hell is a literal place of fire and torment. Others interpret it as the absence of God’s love and presence — a spiritual suffering rather than a physical one. Some liberal Christians question whether a loving God would condemn anyone to eternal suffering.

Key Fact

Beliefs about the afterlife influence how Christians live. Because they believe in judgement, they try to live morally, follow Jesus’s teachings, help others and avoid sin. The hope of heaven brings comfort in times of suffering, and the possibility of hell motivates them to stay on the right path.

Catholics also believe in purgatory — a state of purification after death where souls are cleansed of their sins before entering heaven. This is not a Protestant belief. Catholics pray for the dead, asking God to release souls from purgatory sooner.

Which of the following is the correct reference for 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God'?
A) Genesis 1:1
B) John 1:1
C) Matthew 28:19
D) Luke 1:37
practice_questions.marks: The correct answer is B. John 1:1 opens with these words about the Word (Logos) being with God from the beginning. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two different Christian beliefs about what happens after death.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: resurrection / judgement / heaven / hell / purgatory (Catholic). [1 mark for two correct answers]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in the afterlife influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Belief in judgement motivates Christians to live morally and follow God’s teachings, because they believe their actions will be assessed by God after death. This influences daily decisions about honesty, kindness and helping others.
• The hope of heaven brings comfort during suffering or bereavement. Christians believe death is not the end, which helps them cope with grief and gives them something positive to look forward to.
• Belief in hell acts as a deterrent — Christians try to avoid sin because they believe persistent rejection of God leads to eternal separation from him.
• Catholics pray for the dead, believing prayers can help souls in purgatory reach heaven sooner. This influences their worship practices.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about creation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• God created the world from nothing. Genesis 1:1–3 states: ‘In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth’ and ‘the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters.’ This shows both God the Father and the Holy Spirit were involved in creation. (1–2 marks)
• The Word (Jesus/the Son) was involved in creation. John 1:1–3 states: ‘Through him all things were made; without him nothing was made that has been made.’ This means Jesus existed before creation and was the agent through whom God created everything. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied for additional marks. (1–2 marks)
Two beliefs, each explained and supported by a named source. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The Bible’s account of creation is too outdated to be believed today.’
Evaluate this statement considering arguments for and against. In your response you should:
• refer to Christian teachings
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the statement:
• Scientific evidence (Big Bang, evolution) contradicts a literal six-day creation. Most scientists accept the Earth is billions of years old, not thousands.
• Some argue Genesis was written for an ancient audience and reflects their understanding of the world, not modern scientific knowledge.
• The creation accounts in Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 appear to contradict each other, suggesting they are not literal historical records.
Arguments against the statement:
• Literalist Christians believe the Bible is the direct word of God and therefore without error. Genesis describes exactly what happened.
• Liberal Christians argue the creation accounts are not meant to be scientific — they teach important truths about WHY God created (out of love) and humanity’s special place in creation.
• Many Christians accept science and faith together — Pope Francis said the Big Bang and evolution are real but God is behind them. The accounts are not ‘outdated’ because their purpose is theological, not scientific.
• John 1:1–3 reinforces the importance of the Word in creation, giving it theological depth beyond a simple historical account.
Top band (10-12): Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view. Logical reasoning supported by knowledge. References to religion.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasoned consideration of different points of view with reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Max Level 2 if no religion reference.
Lower band (1-3): Point of view with reason(s).
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in judgement influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Christians try to live morally because they believe God will judge their actions after death. The parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25) teaches that those who helped others will be welcomed into God’s kingdom, motivating Christians to do good.
• Belief in judgement gives Christians a sense of justice — even if wrongdoers escape punishment in this life, God will hold them accountable. This brings comfort when they witness injustice.
• Some Christians are motivated to evangelise (spread the faith) because they believe accepting Jesus is necessary for a favourable judgement.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

before.content_html:
The Incarnation

The incarnation is the Christian belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ. The word literally means “made flesh.” Christians believe that Jesus was not just a good teacher or prophet — he was God the Son taking on a human body to live among people on Earth.

John 1:14 states: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.” This connects directly to John 1:1, which says the Word was God. So the Word (God the Son) who created all things became a human being — Jesus of Nazareth. This is one of the most important beliefs in Christianity.

Key Fact

Christians believe Jesus is both fully God and fully human. He was not half-God and half-human, nor God pretending to be human. He experienced everything humans experience — hunger, tiredness, pain, temptation — while also being divine. This is affirmed in the Nicene Creed: “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.”

Jesus as the Son of God

Christians call Jesus the Son of God, meaning he has a unique relationship with God the Father. This is not meant literally — God did not have a child in the human sense. Rather, it means Jesus shares God’s divine nature and has existed with the Father for all eternity.

Several events in the Gospels confirm Jesus as the Son of God:

  • At Jesus’s baptism, a voice from heaven said: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).
  • At the transfiguration, God’s voice again declared: “This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!” (Mark 9:7).
  • Jesus performed miracles — healing the sick, calming storms, raising the dead — demonstrating divine power.

The incarnation is significant for several reasons. It shows that God loves humanity enough to become one of us. It means God understands human suffering from personal experience. It also means that Jesus’s teachings carry the full authority of God — when Jesus speaks, God speaks. Finally, it was necessary for salvation: only someone who was both God and human could bridge the gap between a holy God and sinful humanity.

The Crucifixion

The crucifixion refers to the death of Jesus on a Roman cross. Jesus was arrested, tried, and sentenced to death by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. He was nailed to a cross and died on a Friday, now commemorated as Good Friday.

Christians believe the crucifixion was not simply a tragic execution — it was part of God’s plan to save humanity from sin. Jesus willingly gave up his life as a sacrifice. Before his arrest, Jesus prayed: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42), showing he accepted his suffering as the Father’s will.

Key Fact

Christians believe Jesus’s death on the cross paid the price for human sin. Because Jesus was sinless, his death was a perfect sacrifice that restored the relationship between God and humanity. This is why the cross is the most important symbol in Christianity.

The Resurrection

The resurrection is the belief that Jesus rose from the dead three days after his crucifixion. On Easter Sunday, women visiting Jesus’s tomb found it empty. An angel told them: “He is not here; he has risen!” (Matthew 28:6). Jesus then appeared to his disciples over 40 days.

The resurrection is the most important event in Christianity. St Paul wrote: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christianity falls apart.

It proves Jesus is the Son of God. Only God could conquer death. The resurrection confirms that Jesus truly was divine.

It shows God’s power over death. Death is not the end — God has the power to raise the dead. This gives Christians hope that they too will be resurrected.

It confirms the promise of eternal life. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die” (John 11:25).

It is the basis of Christian worship. Christians worship on Sunday because it is the day Jesus rose. Easter is the most important festival in the Christian calendar.

The Ascension

Forty days after the resurrection, Jesus ascended (went up) to heaven. Acts 1:9 describes how “he was taken up before their very eyes, and a cloud hid him from their sight.” Two angels then told the disciples that Jesus would return in the same way.

The ascension is significant because it shows Jesus’s mission on Earth was complete. He returned to the Father, where Christians believe he sits “at the right hand of God” (the Nicene Creed) — a position of honour and authority. The ascension also prepared the way for the Holy Spirit to come at Pentecost, empowering the disciples to spread the Christian message. Christians believe Jesus will return from heaven at the end of time to judge the living and the dead.

Key Fact

The events of Jesus’s life form a connected sequence: the incarnation (God becomes human), the crucifixion (Jesus dies for sin), the resurrection (Jesus conquers death), and the ascension (Jesus returns to heaven). Each event is essential to the Christian understanding of salvation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the incarnation?
A) Jesus ascending to heaven
B) God becoming human in Jesus
C) Jesus rising from the dead
D) The Holy Spirit descending on the disciples
practice_questions.marks: The correct answer is B. The incarnation is the belief that God became human (took flesh) in the person of Jesus Christ. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give the name of the event where Jesus returned to heaven after the resurrection.
practice_questions.marks: The ascension. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in the resurrection influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The resurrection gives Christians hope that death is not the end. They believe they too will be raised to new life, which brings comfort during bereavement and in the face of their own mortality.
• Christians worship on Sunday because it is the day Jesus rose from the dead. The resurrection shapes the pattern of Christian worship and makes Easter the most important festival in the Christian calendar.
• The resurrection confirms that Jesus is the Son of God, which strengthens Christians’ faith and commitment to following his teachings.
• St Paul wrote ‘If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile’ (1 Corinthians 15:17) — the resurrection is the foundation of everything Christians believe.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about the incarnation. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• God became human in Jesus Christ. John 1:14 states: ‘The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.’ The ‘Word’ refers to God the Son, who took on human form to live among people. This shows God’s love for humanity. (1–2 marks)
• Jesus is both fully God and fully human. The Nicene Creed affirms Jesus as ‘God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.’ He was not half-God or God pretending to be human, but genuinely both. This was necessary for salvation — only someone who was both could bridge the gap between God and humanity. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied for additional marks. (1–2 marks)
Two beliefs with named sources of authority. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The resurrection of Jesus is the most important Christian belief.’
Evaluate this statement considering arguments for and against. In your response you should:
• refer to Christian teachings
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the statement:
• St Paul wrote ‘If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile’ (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christianity would have no foundation.
• The resurrection proves Jesus is the Son of God. Only God could conquer death, confirming Jesus’s divine nature.
• It gives Christians the promise of eternal life — ‘I am the resurrection and the life’ (John 11:25). Without this hope, the Christian message loses its power.
• It is the reason Christians worship on Sundays and celebrate Easter as their most important festival.
Arguments against the statement:
• The incarnation could be seen as more important — without God becoming human, none of the other events (crucifixion, resurrection) would have happened.
• The crucifixion is when salvation actually happened — Jesus’s death paid the price for sin. Without the sacrifice, the resurrection would have less meaning.
• Some Christians might argue that the teachings of Jesus are most important — the Sermon on the Mount and the parables guide how Christians live daily.
• Others argue that all the events are interconnected and equally important — you cannot separate incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection and ascension.
Top band (10-12): Well-argued response with different viewpoints, logical reasoning, religion references.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasoned consideration with religion references.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Max Level 2 if no religion.
Lower band (1-3): Point of view with reason(s).
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in the incarnation influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Christians believe God understands human suffering because Jesus experienced it personally during the incarnation. This brings comfort when Christians face difficulties — they believe God truly knows what they are going through.
• Because Jesus was God in human form, his teachings carry divine authority. Christians follow his moral teachings (love your neighbour, forgive others) because they believe these come directly from God.
• The incarnation shows God values human life enough to become part of it. This influences Christians to respect and care for all human beings, seeing every person as precious to God.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

before.content_html:
What Is Sin?

Sin is any thought or action that goes against God’s will. Christians believe sin damages the relationship between humans and God. Every time a person sins, they move further away from God. Sin can take many forms — lying, stealing, hatred, selfishness, envy and many others.

Christians believe all humans are sinful. Nobody is perfect, and everyone falls short of God’s standards. St Paul wrote: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). This is a problem because God is holy and just — sin cannot exist in God’s presence. Humans therefore need to be saved from the consequences of their sin.

Original Sin

Original sin is the belief that all humans are born with a built-in tendency to do wrong. This idea comes from the story of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3. God placed Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden and told them not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. The serpent tempted Eve, she ate the fruit, and Adam followed.

Key Fact

Adam and Eve’s disobedience is called the Fall. Christians believe this act of disobedience broke the perfect relationship between God and humanity. As a result, all humans are born with a tendency to sin — this is original sin. It is not a specific sin a person commits, but a condition inherited from the first humans.

Catholic view: Original sin is washed away through the sacrament of baptism. This is one reason Catholics baptise infants — to free the baby from original sin as early as possible. Even after baptism, humans still have a tendency to sin (called concupiscence).

Protestant view: Most Protestants accept the concept of original sin but emphasise that salvation comes through faith in Jesus rather than through sacraments. Some Protestants do not practise infant baptism, believing a person must choose to follow Christ for themselves.

Liberal view: Some liberal Christians see the story of Adam and Eve as a myth that teaches an important truth — humans have a natural tendency to do wrong — rather than a literal historical event. The lesson is the same: humans need God’s help to overcome sin.

What Is Salvation?

Salvation means being saved from sin and its consequences — ultimately, being granted eternal life with God rather than eternal separation from God. Christians believe humans cannot save themselves because all are sinful. They need God’s help.

the specification identifies three means of salvation: law, grace and Spirit. Different Christian traditions emphasise these differently.

Salvation Through Law

Some Christians believe that following God’s laws — the Ten Commandments and the moral teachings of Jesus — is essential for salvation. By obeying God’s commands, a person shows they are devoted to God and deserving of eternal life. Catholics especially emphasise the importance of good works alongside faith — the Epistle of James states: “Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead” (James 2:17).

Salvation Through Grace

Grace is the free, undeserved gift of God’s love. Christians believe God offers salvation not because humans deserve it, but because God loves them. Ephesians 2:8–9 states: “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith — and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God — not by works, so that no one can boast.”

Key Fact

Protestants, especially those in the Reformed tradition, emphasise salvation by grace alone through faith alone. Humans cannot earn salvation by doing good deeds — it is a free gift from God, received through faith in Jesus Christ. Catholics believe both faith and works are necessary — grace enables good works, and both contribute to salvation.

Salvation Through the Holy Spirit

Christians believe the Holy Spirit plays an active role in salvation. The Spirit works within believers to help them recognise their sin, turn towards God, and live a holy life. Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians particularly emphasise the role of the Holy Spirit, believing it gives spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues, prophecy and healing.

The Holy Spirit guides Christians in daily life, helping them make good decisions and resist temptation. Jesus promised: “The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26). The Spirit also brings comfort in suffering, strengthens faith in difficult times, and empowers Christians to share the gospel with others.

The Role of Christ in Salvation

All Christians agree that Jesus Christ is central to salvation. Without Jesus, humans would remain trapped in sin with no way back to God. Jesus’s death and resurrection made salvation possible.

Atonement

Atonement literally means “at-one-ment” — making God and humanity “at one” again. It is the belief that Jesus’s death on the cross restored the broken relationship between God and humans caused by sin. Through his sacrifice, Jesus took the punishment that humans deserved.

Key Fact

Isaiah 53:5 prophesied the atonement: “He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” Christians believe this prophecy was fulfilled by Jesus on the cross.

Substitutionary atonement: Jesus took the place of sinful humans and bore the punishment they deserved. He was a substitute — dying instead of humanity. This view is common among evangelical Protestants.

Satisfaction theory: Human sin offended God’s honour and justice. Only a perfect sacrifice could satisfy God’s justice. Jesus, being sinless, was the only one who could offer this perfect payment. This view is associated with Anselm of Canterbury and is the foundational Catholic/Thomistic atonement model. Note: the penal substitution view described above is a distinctly Protestant teaching, rooted in Luther and Calvin; Anselm's satisfaction theory differs in mechanism (paying an honour-debt, not a penal penalty).

Moral example: Some liberal Christians see Jesus’s death less as a payment for sin and more as a supreme example of self-sacrificing love. His willingness to die inspires Christians to live selflessly and sacrificially for others.

Regardless of which understanding they hold, all Christians agree that the atonement makes salvation available. Jesus’s sacrifice opened the door for humans to be reconciled with God, forgiven for their sins, and given the promise of eternal life.
before.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark evaluation questions on salvation, you will often need to discuss whether faith or works (or both) are more important. A strong answer will show you understand the Protestant view (grace alone through faith alone, Ephesians 2:8–9) and the Catholic view (faith and works together, James 2:17). Always include specific Bible references or teachings to support each side — this is what moves you from Level 2 to Level 3 and above.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'original sin'?
A) The first sin a person commits as a child
B) The tendency to sin inherited from Adam and Eve
C) The sin of not going to church
D) A sin that cannot be forgiven
practice_questions.marks: The correct answer is B. Original sin is the built-in tendency to do wrong that all humans inherit from Adam and Eve’s disobedience in the Garden of Eden. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name one means of salvation identified in Christian teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Any one from: law / grace / the Holy Spirit. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in salvation influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Christians try to follow God’s laws and the teachings of Jesus because they believe obedience to God is part of how they achieve salvation. This motivates moral behaviour and charitable actions in daily life.
• Belief that salvation is a free gift of grace gives Christians a sense of gratitude and humility. They feel they do not deserve God’s love but receive it anyway, which motivates them to show the same grace and forgiveness to others.
• Christians who emphasise the Holy Spirit’s role seek a personal relationship with God through prayer and worship, believing the Spirit guides them towards salvation.
• The belief that Jesus died for their sins gives Christians confidence that they can be forgiven, encouraging them to repent when they do wrong rather than giving up.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about atonement. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Jesus’s death on the cross restored the relationship between God and humanity. Isaiah 53:5 states: ‘He was pierced for our transgressions… by his wounds we are healed.’ Christians believe Jesus took the punishment humans deserved for their sins, making reconciliation with God possible. (1–2 marks)
• Jesus was a substitute for sinful humanity — he died in our place. Romans 5:8 states: ‘God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.’ This shows atonement is an act of God’s love, not something humans earned. (1–2 marks)
• Source named and applied to support each belief. (1–2 marks)
Two beliefs with named sources. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Good works are more important than faith for achieving salvation.’
Evaluate this statement considering arguments for and against. In your response you should:
• refer to Christian teachings
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the statement:
• James 2:17 states ‘Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.’ This suggests that believing in God is not enough — Christians must also act on their beliefs.
• Catholics teach that good works are essential alongside faith. The sacraments (baptism, Eucharist) and acts of charity contribute to salvation.
• In the parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25), those who helped the hungry, thirsty and sick were saved. This seems to prioritise actions over beliefs.
Arguments against the statement:
• Ephesians 2:8–9 states salvation is ‘by grace… through faith — not by works, so that no one can boast.’ Protestants argue salvation is a free gift that cannot be earned.
• The criminal crucified next to Jesus was promised paradise despite having no time for good works (Luke 23:43). This shows faith alone is sufficient.
• Martin Luther argued that humans are saved by faith alone (sola fide). Good works are a natural result of faith, not a condition for salvation.
• Some argue faith and works cannot be separated — genuine faith naturally produces good actions.
Top band (10-12): Well-argued, multiple viewpoints, religion references, justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasoned consideration with religion references.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Reasoned point of view. Max Level 2 without religion.
Lower band (1-3): Point of view with reason(s).
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in original sin influences Christians today.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Catholics practise infant baptism to wash away original sin. They believe it is important to baptise babies as soon as possible so the child is freed from this inherited condition and welcomed into the Church.
• Belief in original sin reminds Christians that they are not perfect and will always be tempted to do wrong. This influences them to be humble, to regularly confess their sins, and to depend on God’s grace rather than their own efforts.
• Original sin explains why the world is imperfect and why humans need a saviour. This strengthens Christians’ belief in the necessity of Jesus and motivates them to follow his teachings.
Two clear, developed points needed for full marks. [4 marks]
